claims.text: Protective oxide development and retention in high-entropy alloys is governed by inherently sluggish diffusion in the multi-principal-element matrix.
Sluggish matrix diffusion moderates the outward transport of passivating elements such as Al.
Slower outward Al migration promotes selective oxidation into a compact, slow-growing Al2O3 scale.
Al2O3 provides substantial resistance to high-temperature oxidation and grows more slowly than chromium oxide.
Cr2O3 can provide a compact protective scale with superior oxidation resistance.
A continuous Al2O3 and/or Cr2O3 layer limits oxidation by impeding oxygen ingress and metal-cation egress.
The relevant initial material can be a single-phase, Al-containing, multicomponent HEA in an as-cast or thermally homogenized state.
Isothermal exposure in air or oxygen at 900–1100 °C for tens to hundreds of hours will reveal protective-scale formation.
Relative to a reduced-Al HEA or a conventional faster-diffusing alloy, the proposed HEA will have a lower oxidation rate and reduced weight gain.
Relative to the baseline, the proposed HEA will form a more uniform and adherent oxide scale.
Relative to the baseline, the proposed HEA will exhibit less internal oxidation and substrate degradation.
Protective behavior requires sufficient concentrations of strong oxide-forming elements such as Al or Cr.
Chromia protection can be undermined above 900 °C by formation of volatile CrO3.
Mn can promote non-protective Mn-rich oxides and worsen HEA oxidation resistance.
Complex HEA chemistry, surface heterogeneity, microstructure, and high-temperature phase instability can alter the resulting oxide structure.
Different microstructural states may produce enough diffusion to override nominal sluggish-diffusion behavior.
A higher-Al HEA should exhibit both slower oxidation and a denser Al2O3-rich scale than a lower-Al HEA under otherwise identical oxidation conditions.
Failure of higher Al to reduce oxidation, failure to form a compact protective scale, or absence of a diffusion-rate distinction would falsify the proposed mechanism.
